How to Play Catan: Rules in the Order That Makes Sense

2026-09-25

How to play Catan: be the first player to reach 10 victory points. That is the whole game. It plays 3 to 4 people in about 75 minutes. Everything else, the trading, the building, the robber, is just the path to that number.

I have taught this game at least 20 times, and every group hits the same wall. The rulebook teaches pieces first: here are the tiles, the roads, the settlements, the cards. By the time you reach your first turn, nothing connects. So here is Catan in the order it actually clicks. Explain it like this and your table is playing in five minutes.

The Goal and the Island

The map is 19 hexes. Five of them produce resources: hills make brick, forest makes lumber, mountains make ore, fields make grain, pasture makes wool. The desert makes nothing, and the robber sits there at the start.

Each hex gets a number token from 2 to 12, except 7. When the dice roll that number, that hex produces. Every settlement and city you own bordering it collects: 1 card per settlement, 2 per city. Your starting position tells you which resources you will see all game.

Setup in 60 Seconds

Everyone places 2 settlements and 2 roads. Settlements go on corners where three hexes meet. Roads go on the edges between them. One rule matters more than any other: the distance rule. No settlement may sit next to another settlement, not even your own, because every future settlement needs the same two-corner gap.

Here is the part most guides mess up: your second settlement pays you. Every hex touching that second settlement gives you 1 resource card immediately, and it is marked with a star in the rulebook precisely so you do not miss it. You begin the game with 2 victory points and a small hand of cards. It is a game with a 10 point finish line where the score already reads 2:2:2:2.

Your Turn: Roll, Trade, Build

You do three things in order. First, roll both dice. The total decides which hexes produce, and everyone collects at once, not just the roller. Then trade. Then build.

Trading has two flavors. Domestic trade: on your turn you can swap cards with any other player, and anyone can make you an offer. Maritime trade: the bank always accepts 4 identical cards for any 1 card you want, and a settlement on a harbor improves the ratio to 3:1, or 2:1 for the resource that harbor shows.

Building costs are the only numbers you need to memorize:

Road: 1 brick, 1 lumber. Settlement: 1 brick, 1 lumber, 1 wool, 1 grain. City: 3 ore, 2 grain. Development card: 1 ore, 1 wool, 1 grain.

Pay attention to this number: a city takes 3 ore and 2 grain, and it doubles the production of that spot. Two cities and two settlements are already 6 of your 10 points. Cities are how a slow trickle becomes an engine.

Then Comes the Robber

When a 7 rolls, nobody collects. First, everyone holding more than 7 cards discards half, rounded down. 9 cards means you toss 4. Then the roller moves the robber to any other hex, shutting that hex off until the robber leaves, and steals 1 random card from a player with a building on the new hex.

The 7 comes up 17% of rolls, more than any other number. That is why nobody plays a single-resource strategy safely for long. The robber exists to keep the leader honest.

The Points Hiding in Cards

Development cards cost ore, wool, and grain, and the deck holds 25: 14 knights, 5 victory points, 6 progress cards. Knights are the muscle. Play 3 and you take the Largest Army card, worth 2 victory points. Build one road of at least 5 segments and you take Longest Road, also worth 2.

Here is why that matters. Both of those points can be stolen, and the swing is 4 victory points in a single turn. A game that looks over at 8 points can flip before the winner even announces it, and you only win on your turn, so secrecy is a legal weapon. Hoard a victory point card until you can declare 10 in one motion.

Here is the part nobody tells you: the dice do not decide Catan. Your starting placement does. I won my first game by luck and then lost ten in a row, and it took a patient friend to show me why. A 6 or 8 rolls 14% of the time. A 5 or 9 rolls 11%. A 2 or 12 rolls 3%. Your two starting settlements sit on six numbers for the rest of the game, and those percentages never change. The best players win in the first 60 seconds, before the first roll, because nobody can fix a bad start later. Mix your starting resources: brick and lumber build roads and settlements early, ore and grain build cities late. Most beginners pick pretty spots and then spend the whole game watching a neighbor collect cards.

What to Buy, and What to Skip

So now you know how to play. The next question is which box to put on the table.

The base Catan game covers 3 to 4 players and runs about 75 minutes. It is the version everyone means when they say Catan, and the full details live on my Catan page. Note the player count: the base box needs at least 3 people, so it is a game night game, not a date night game. If your game night usually pulls 5 or 6 people, the 5-6 player expansion adds a special building phase between turns so the bigger group stays busy. Honest note: more players means a longer game and sharper elbows.

If your group is not into hard negotiation, or you want something calmer, Carcassonne is the other classic gateway game. Same one-small-decision-per-turn magic, no robber robbing you. 2 to 5 players, 35 minutes, a totally different mood, and my Carcassonne page has the details. I keep both on my shelf and reach for them on different nights.

And if you fall for the base game hard, Cities & Knights is the expansion that turns Catan into a real engine game. Skip it until the base game feels solved. That takes a while.

The Honest Truth About Catan

The dice can leave you stuck. Bad rolls, a robber parked on your best hex, and you coast through twenty minutes with nothing to build while everyone else sprints. It is the game's most famous annoyance, and it is real.

But it is also the engine. The desperation is what makes a trade feel like a real deal and comebacks feel like miracles. If your group hates being denied turns, you will feel this one. If your group loves drama, you will love it.

Here is the Shelf Test. Would this game survive ten plays on your shelf? Catan is the rare game that survives a hundred. I have played it with gamers, grandparents, and people who swear they hate board games, and it is still the first thing I teach a new player. The base game is $39.99 tonight and it bounces between $35 and $50 depending on the week. Under $40 is a fair deal. For a bigger group, the expansion runs about $25 to $35. Grab the box, use the setup order above, and let the first player to 10 points brag forever.
